extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of crystallography, mineralogists, gemologists, and physical scientists studying crystal properties
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and classificatory criteria for crystal structure, mechanical and optical properties, and methods used to determine symmetry and physical behaviour of crystals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sohncke point-system criterion for crystal repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient that each molecule of an indefinitely extended crystal, represented by its 'point' (or centre of gravity), is identically situated with respect to the molecules surrounding it; the lattice-structure of Bravais is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of possible regular point-systems yields sixty-five arrangements (Sohncke). These may be obtained from the fourteen Bravais space-lattices by interpenetrating identical lattices, provided the resulting structure conforms with the homogeneity characteristic of crystals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete classification of crystal symmetry (32 classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sohncke's point-systems together with mirror-image (enantiomorphous) repetition give the whole thirty-two classes of crystal symmetry, and 230 distinct types of crystal structure fall into these classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work of Fedorov, Schoenflies and Barlow independently showed how point-system theory explains the 32 classes; missing forms are enantiomorphs introduced by mirror repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a crystal as interpenetrating regular point-systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A crystal consists of a finite number of interpenetrating regular point-systems, which all possess like and like-directed coincidence movements. Each separate point-system is occupied by similar material particles, but these may be different for the different interpenetrating partial systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative phrasing: a crystal consists of n interpenetrating regular point-systems each formed of similar atoms; space-lattices of the combined system are geometrically identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal-external symmetry correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Many physical properties of crystals vary with direction in the material but are the same in certain directions; these directions obey the same laws of symmetry as do the faces on the exterior of the crystal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the symmetry of the internal structure is the same as the symmetry of the external form; any measured directional property should reflect the crystal's symmetry elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientation-specific measurement of elastic constants
rubrics_metrics.description: Elastic constants of crystals must be determined using bars and plates cut from the crystal with known orientations; the 'elasticity surface' expressing the coefficients in various directions is symmetrical with respect to the same planes and axes of symmetry as the crystal itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For homogeneous elastic deformation (pressure on all sides) compression coefficients surfaces are sphere/spheroid/ellipsoid depending on higher symmetry; recorded elasticity surface must conform to crystal symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between plastic deformation and twinning/glide-plane deformation
rubrics_metrics.description: In plastic deformation the crystalline particles are displaced without any change in their orientation; in the more usual permanent deformation without fracture the particles glide along certain planes into a new (twinned) position of equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pressing a knife into calcite edge produces glide along a plane (110) called a 'glide-plane' and a plane of twinning; secondary twinning appears as repeated lamination in recrystallized materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleavage as direction of minimum cohesion and determinative character
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleavage consists of certain plane directions across which the cohesion is a minimum and along which the crystal may be readily split; these directions are always parallel to a possible face on the crystal and usually one prominently developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleavage directions are symmetrically repeated according to the crystal's symmetry. Cleavage quality is described as perfect, good/distinct, or little/none (e.g., perfect in halite {100}, octahedral {111} cleavage in diamond, none in quartz). Cleavage is of considerable determinative value for mineral identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percussion and pressure figures reflect face symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Percussion figures (linear cracks radiating from a point of impact) and pressure figures produced by pressing a blunt point show rays whose number and orientation agree with the symmetry of the face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On cube faces rays parallel diagonals; on octahedral faces a three-rayed star. Percussion/pressure figures are readily developed in cleavage sheets (e.g., mica).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardness as anisotropic property depending on crystalline structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardness is often defined and measured by the resistance a crystal face offers to scratching and depends largely on crystalline structure; hardness may vary with direction on a crystal face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: graphite (soft) vs diamond (hard). Instruments like the sclerometer attempt quantitative hardness determination; minerals like cyanite show widely different hardness on different faces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etched (corrosion) figures reveal symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: When a crystal is corroded by a solvent, etched figures (minute pits, depressions, elevations bounded by vicinal faces) develop and are extremely important aids in determining the symmetry of crystals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sphere cut from a crystal immersed in acid will be bounded by surfaces approximating crystal faces; etched figures can be produced artificially and may reveal symmetry not evident from external form (e.g., nepheline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by action on plane-polarized light (five optical groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: All crystals may be referred to one of five groups according to their action on transmitted plane-polarized light: (1) optically isotropic (cubic), (2) optically uniaxial (tetragonal and hexagonal), (3) optically biaxial with three principal optical directions coinciding with crystallographic axes (orthorhombic), (4) optically biaxial with one principal direction coinciding with a crystallographic axis (monoclinic), (5) optically biaxial with no fixed definite relation between optical and crystallographic directions (anorthic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The several symmetry-classes of each system are optically the same except rare circularly polarizing substances; use this classification to predict behaviour in polarizing microscopy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniaxial optic axis and birefringence sign (ω and ε)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniaxial crystals have one optic axis; for each colour there are two refractive indices: the ordinary index (ω) and the extraordinary index (ε). If ω > ε the crystal is optically negative; if ω < ε it is optically positive. The difference ω − ε measures the strength of double refraction (birefringence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indices vary with colour and temperature. Optical indicatrix for uniaxial crystals is an ellipsoid of revolution; behaviour in crossed nicols (extinction positions, interference colours) depends on orientation and thickness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicatrix and ray-surface description for uniaxial crystals
rubrics_metrics.description: The optical indicatrix has principal axis proportional to the extraordinary index and equatorial diameters proportional to the ordinary index; the ray-surface consists of two sheets: a sphere (ordinary rays) and an ellipsoid of revolution (extraordinary rays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For positive uniaxial crystals the indicatrix is prolate; for negative it is oblate. Fresnel's ellipsoid and ray-surface geometry explain interference and propagation directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical microscope tests for uniaxial crystals (extinction and interference figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewed between crossed nicols, a uniaxial crystal along the optic axis remains dark when rotated; in other orientations it shows extinction four times per 360° and produces interference colours; in convergent light with the optic axis coincident with the microscope axis an interference figure of concentric coloured rings with a black cross is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a quarter-wave mica plate on the interference figure allows determination of optical sign (positive/negative), useful in distinguishing faceted gemstones (e.g., zircon positive, corundum negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biaxial indicatrix, optic axes and sign (α, β, γ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biaxial crystals have three principal refractive indices α < β < γ; the indicatrix is an ellipsoid with axes proportional to these indices. Two optic axes (primary) exist where rays have same velocity 1/β; the angle between them is the optic axial angle and the acute/obtuse bisectrices define optical sign: acute bisectrix coinciding with γ means optically positive, with α means optically negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The difference γ − α measures strength of birefringence. Fresnel's ray-surface and indicatrix geometry determine interference figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dispersion of optic axes and bisectrices in biaxial/monoclinic crystals
rubrics_metrics.description: Refractive indices vary with colour and temperature causing slight differences in indicatrix and ray-surface; dispersion of optic axes means positions of optic axes and axial angle vary with colour. In monoclinic crystals there may also be dispersion of the bisectrices leading to crossed/horizontal/inclined dispersion types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dispersion type expressed by comparison of axial angles for red vs blue light (ρ and υ); examples: borax, orthoclase, gypsum show the three kinds of dispersion. Dispersion affects interference figure symmetry and may change with temperature (e.g., orthoclase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference-figure diagnostics for biaxial crystals
rubrics_metrics.description: Biaxial interference figures (viewed along the acute bisectrix in convergent light between crossed nicols) show concentric coloured ovals around each optic axis joining to form an 8-shaped loop and outer lemniscate-like rings; rotation causes the central cross to break into hyperbola branches and diagonal positions reveal optic axial angle for measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference figures allow accurate measurement of optic axial angle and identification of optical orientation; often requires cutting plates perpendicular to bisectrix or using cleavage flakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical orientation conventions for orthorhombic crystals
rubrics_metrics.description: In orthorhombic crystals the three principal vibration-directions coincide with the three crystallographic axes and thus have fixed positions; optical orientation is defined by which crystallographic planes the optic axial plane and the acute bisectrix are parallel or perpendicular to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In parallel light between crossed nicols such crystals extinguish parallel to crystallographic axes (straight extinction); interference figures are symmetrical about two lines at right angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monoclinic optical behaviour and extinction directions
rubrics_metrics.description: In monoclinic crystals only one vibration-direction (parallel to the ortho-axis (010)) has fixed position; the other two lie in (010) and may vary with colour and temperature. Straight extinction occurs only in faces/sections perpendicular to the plane of symmetry (010); in other faces extinction directions are inclined to edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Angles between extinction directions and edges are measurable constants characteristic of the substance (e.g., plagioclase). Monoclinic dispersion of bisectrices leads to specific interference figure symmetries (crossed, horizontal, or inclined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anorthic (triclinic) complexity in optical orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: In anorthic crystals there is no relation between optical and crystallographic directions; determination of optical orientation is difficult and dispersion of bisectrices/optic axes is more complex, with interference figures lacking symmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect little or no fixed relation to crystallographic directions; more elaborate optical analysis needed to determine orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleochroism and dichroism/trichroism definitions and detection
rubrics_metrics.description: In non-cubic crystals rays vibrating in different directions are generally differently absorbed; uniaxial crystals with perceptible differences are 'dichroic', biaxial crystals may be 'trichroic' or in general 'pleochroic'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a dichroscope or polarizing microscope (with analyser removed) to observe axial colours separately; dichroscope (Iceland-spar rhombohedron plus prisms) is a simple field instrument for faceted gems and can distinguish isotropic from dichroic stones (e.g., ruby vs spinel-ruby).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular polarization associated with enantiomorphous symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Some crystals (including certain isotropic and uniaxial examples) rotate the plane of polarization of light; such circular polarizing crystals crystallize in symmetry-classes lacking planes and centre of symmetry (enantiomorphous hemihedral forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include sodium chlorate (cubic), quartz (rhombohedral), cinnabar; rotatory power may be lost on dissolution except in special cases (e.g., strychnine sulphate weakly active in solution). Circular polarization is therefore linked to the absence of inversion/mirror symmetry and to enantiomorphism.
